challenges.title: Stack Peek
challenges.author: Wael Hammami
challenges.description:
Your first look at how local variables sit next to each other in memory.

The program reads your name into a 32-byte buffer, then checks a separate integer. Overflow the buffer just enough to overwrite that integer and the program prints the flag.

**Goal:** make the check pass. Source and binary are provided; run it locally.

hints.text: Draw the stack: buffer first, then the integer, then the saved frame pointer.
You need 32 bytes of padding plus the little-endian value the check expects.

challenges.title: Buffer Overflow Baby
challenges.author: Wael Hammami
challenges.description:
No canary, no PIE, NX enabled, and a `win()` function that prints the flag but is never called.

Classic setup: find the offset to the saved return address, then point it at `win`.

**Goal:** redirect execution. `pwntools` recommended.

hints.text: Generate a cyclic pattern, crash it, read the offset from the fault address.
`win` is at a fixed address because PIE is off. Check `objdump -d`.

challenges.title: Format String Warmup
challenges.author: Salma Ferchichi
challenges.description:
The program does `printf(user_input)` with no format constant. The flag is loaded into a local buffer that never gets printed.

**Goal:** use `%p` and positional specifiers to walk the stack until you find the flag, then make `printf` print it as a string.

hints.text: `%p %p %p %p %p %p %p %p` prints eight stack slots at a time.
Once you find the index of the flag, `%<index>$s` prints it as a string.

challenges.title: ret2win, with a Twist
challenges.author: Wael Hammami
challenges.description:
`win()` now takes two arguments, and the binary has exactly one usable gadget: `pop rdi; pop rsi; ret`. PIE is off, NX is on, and there is still no canary.

**Goal:** build a ROP chain that calls `win(0x1337, 0x2026)` and prints the flag.

hints.text: Find the gadget with `ROPgadget --binary twist | grep "pop rdi"`.
The stack layout is 64 bytes of buffer, 8 bytes of saved rbp, then the return address. Two arguments follow the gadget address.

challenges.title: One Byte at a Time
challenges.author: Wael Hammami
challenges.description:
A service compares your guess to the flag with an early-exit loop and answers in constant time — almost. The comparison itself leaks a few microseconds per matching prefix.

A Python harness that simulates the service locally is provided, including a calibrated noise model. No network target is involved.

**Goal:** recover the flag with a statistically sound timing attack.

hints.text: Average hundreds of samples per candidate byte; the signal is smaller than the noise.
Compare candidate timings against the current best, not against an absolute threshold.
